issues.legal_issue: The term law for purposes of rejecting a plaint includes binding judicial precedent.
material_facts: The defendants applied to reject the plaint on the ground that a binding Supreme Court decision prescribed the remedy for challenging the award and barred the civil suit.
The plaintiffs argued that the term law in the plaint-rejection provision referred only to legislation, not judicial decisions.
issues.conclusion: The term law includes binding judicial precedent, so a precedent that bars a claim may support rejection of a plaint.
issues.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits rejection where a suit appears from the plaint to be barred by law; law includes judicial precedent. The Court relied on Article 141 of the Constitution and agreed with Virender Kumar Dixit v. State of U.P., Hermes Marines Ltd. v. Capeshore Maritime Partners F.Z.C., Shahid S. Sarkar v. Usha Ramrao Bhojane, and Mira Sinha v. State of Jharkhand.

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applied for rejection of a civil plaint on the ground that the claim was barred.
predicates.binding_higher_court_precedent_bars_clai: A binding decision of a higher court prescribes a route for the claim that excludes the action brought.

issues.definition: When a defendant seeks rejection of a plaint and a binding higher-court decision bars the action brought, that decision counts as law for plaint rejection.

issues.legal_issue: A civil suit cannot be used to challenge an award recording a settlement reached by the parties before a Lok Adalat, even when the challenge alleges fraud or misrepresentation.
material_facts: The parties to a pending civil suit signed a joint compromise petition, which the Lok Adalat accepted and recorded in an award disposing of the suit.
Some parties later filed a civil suit seeking to have the award declared void and not binding, alleging fraud and misrepresentation.
The defendants applied for rejection of the plaint; the trial court rejected it, but the High Court restored the suit.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit was barred; the only remedy to challenge the award was a petition under Article 226 and/or Article 227 of the Constitution, on limited grounds. The Court restored the order rejecting the plaint and left the plaintiffs free to pursue that writ remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 21 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, the award followed a written settlement signed by the parties. State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh held that an award based on a settlement is final and binding, is executable as a decree, and may be challenged only by a petition under Article 226 and/or Article 227 on limited grounds. The Court held that this rule applied despite allegations of fraud or misrepresentation, and relied on Article 141 and M. Nagaraj v. Union of India for the binding force of Supreme Court decisions. The plaint was therefore rejectable under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_settlement_award: A plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking to invalidate an award made by a dispute-resolution forum.
predicates.award_records_signed_party_compromise: The award records a compromise signed by the parties to the dispute.
predicates.binding_precedent_confines_challenge_to_: A binding higher-court decision limits challenges to this kind of award to a constitutional writ proceeding.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges an award recording a signed party compromise and binding precedent confines challenges to a writ proceeding, the civil suit is barred and the writ proceeding is the only challenge route.
